html:
The Plain of Jars is a landscape of thousands of large stone jars on the Xiangkhouang plateau in northern Laos. The jars, carved from sandstone and other rock, stand in groups of one to several hundred, some up to about three metres tall. They date to the Iron Age, roughly between 500 BCE and 500 CE.

Their purpose is linked to death. The French archaeologist Madeleine Colani, who studied them in the 1930s, found human bones, beads and burnt remains nearby and thought the jars held bodies while they decayed, before the bones were buried. Later digs found burials around the jars. Local legend says giants made them to brew rice wine.

The plateau lay on trade routes between the Mekong valley and the coast of Vietnam. During the Laotian Civil War it was heavily bombed by the United States, and unexploded bombs still lie in the fields, so only cleared sites can be visited. UNESCO listed the jars as a World Heritage Site in 2019.
